parsed.thesis: In any system with a persistent authoritative artifact, ground truth resides in the artifact's observable content—not in session memory, version metadata, or derived state. Every merge, monitoring claim (including 'no change'), and downstream broadcast must verify against the source itself; human corrections must be immediately hardened into enforced verification gates and propagated to all derived states, or stale information will silently survive and be re-exposed.

principleCandidate.title: Source primacy: verify artifact content, not memory or metadata, before merges and claims
principleCandidate.rationale: The root cause was treating session memory, version numbers, and line counts as proxies for truth: a stale 08:12 session record overwrote the user's 08:24 source-file correction, and three inspection rounds claimed 'no change' without reading the source, letting one error propagate for hours and be re-corrected twice. Mandating actual source verification (mtime plus content comparison) with the source as final authority—and converting first corrections into automated gates that propagate to derived states—cuts every path by which stale data survives: merging, inspection, and broadcast.
principleCandidate.scope: Applies whenever cached, derived, or session state is merged with, synchronized against, or reported from a persistent authoritative artifact: cross-session state merges, periodic inspections and no-change assertions, pre-broadcast consistency checks, and the aftermath of any human correction to an authoritative source.

risks: Substantially overlaps existing axiom T-03 (use observable evidence before inferring causes or claiming results) and partially with T-05, T-08, and T-10; adopting it as a new axiom risks redundancy unless framed as an operational extension of those axioms.
Hashing or fully comparing large files on every heartbeat or inspection adds performance overhead; may require change-detection optimization or sampling, which could reintroduce verification gaps.

Treating the 'source file' as unconditionally authoritative fails when the source itself is corrupted, ambiguous, or when multiple candidate authorities conflict; a conflict-resolution rule is needed.
Hard mandatory gates can block or delay urgent workflows when verification tooling is unavailable; fail-safe behavior (halt-and-alert rather than proceed-on-stale) must be defined to avoid deadlocks.
Alerting on mtime changes alone risks alert fatigue from trivial touches; content-hash comparison mitigates this but increases implementation complexity.

principleDraft.title: Source primacy: verify source content, not memory or metadata, before merges and claims
principleDraft.statement: Whenever an agent merges, synchronizes with, inspects, or reports from a persistent authoritative artifact, it must read and compare the artifact's actual content (e.g., mtime plus content or hash comparison) as the final authority, never accepting session memory, version numbers, line counts, or derived state as proof of truth. A 'no change' assertion is a claim and requires the same direct source read as any change claim. When a human corrects the authoritative source, the correction must be immediately hardened into an enforced verification gate (the operation halts on mismatch rather than proceeding on stale data) and propagated to all derived states—caches, copies, and downstream broadcasts—before those states are reused or re-broadcast.
principleDraft.rationale: The failure chain was sustained by treating proxies for truth as truth: a stale 08:12 session record overwrote the user's 08:24 source-file correction, and three inspection rounds asserted 'no change' without reading the source, letting one error propagate for hours and be re-corrected twice. Requiring direct source-content verification at every merge, inspection, and broadcast closes every proxy path by which stale data survives; hardening the first correction into an enforced gate and propagating it to derived states prevents the same stale information from being silently re-exposed downstream.
applicability: Cross-session or cross-agent state merges where cached or remembered state is combined with or written to a persistent authoritative artifact
Periodic inspections, monitoring checks, or heartbeat reviews of an authoritative artifact, including any assertion of 'no change'
Pre-broadcast or pre-publish consistency checks before propagating artifact content to derived states or downstream consumers
Immediately after any human correction to an authoritative source, when caches, copies, or downstream consumers of that source exist
antiPatterns: Merging or overwriting authoritative source content based on session memory, cached records, or remembered versions without re-reading the source
Asserting 'no change' from version numbers, line counts, or metadata without comparing actual source content
Broadcasting or reusing derived state that was not re-verified against the authoritative source after a known human correction
Re-accepting the same human correction repeatedly instead of converting the first correction into an enforced verification gate
Treating derived or cached state as authoritative when it conflicts with the source artifact

intentContract.ownerIntent: Prevent stale session memory or metadata from overwriting or masking corrections made to the authoritative source artifact, and stop 'no change' claims asserted without reading the source itself.
intentContract.targetBehavior: Before every merge, periodic inspection (including no-change assertions), or downstream broadcast involving a persistent authoritative artifact, the agent visibly reads or hashes the artifact's current content, treats it as the final authority on conflict, and upon detecting a human correction refreshes all derived states and installs a verification gate that halts the operation on mismatch.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Overwriting or contradicting the authoritative source using stale session memory, version metadata, or line counts; claiming 'no change' without reading the source; re-broadcasting derived state that was not re-verified after a correction; repeatedly re-accepting the same human correction instead of enforcing a gate.
intentContract.evidenceSource: A stale 08:12 session record overwrote the user's 08:24 source-file correction; three inspection rounds claimed 'no change' without reading the source; the error propagated for hours and was re-corrected twice.
intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should demand tool-trajectory evidence that the source file's content was actually read or hashed before each merge and before each no-change claim, that post-correction derived states were re-verified or refreshed rather than reused, and that a detected mismatch halts the operation with an alert instead of proceeding on stale data.

risks: Substantial overlap with core axiom T-03 (observable evidence before claims) and partial overlap with T-05 (guardrails), T-08 (feedback hardening), and T-10 (persisting state outside transient context); this principle must be framed and adopted as an operational extension of those axioms for artifact merges, no-change claims, and broadcast propagation, or it risks redundancy in the axiom set.

Hashing or fully comparing large files on every inspection or heartbeat adds performance overhead; optimizations like sampling or change-detection shortcuts could silently reintroduce verification gaps.

Treating the 'source file' as unconditionally authoritative fails when the source itself is corrupted, ambiguous, or when multiple candidate authorities conflict; a conflict-resolution and escalation rule is needed before the gate can be safely enforced.

Hard mandatory gates can block or delay urgent workflows when verification tooling is unavailable; fail-safe behavior must be defined as halt-and-alert rather than proceed-on-stale, while avoiding deadlock on repeated tooling failure.
Alerting on mtime changes alone risks alert fatigue from trivial touches; requiring content-hash comparison to suppress false alerts increases implementation complexity.

Applying the principle to transient or non-authoritative artifacts (where no persistent source of truth exists) would force pointless verification work; applicability must be scoped to systems with a designated authoritative artifact.

principleDraft.statement: Whenever a merge, synchronization, inspection, or broadcast touches a persistent authoritative artifact, the artifact's actual content — verified by reading it and comparing mtime plus content, never by version number, line count, or session memory — is the final authority. Before merging any cross-session or historical record, before asserting 'no change', and before broadcasting content derived from state, the agent must verify against the current source and resolve any discrepancy in the source's favor. When a human corrects the authoritative source, that correction must immediately propagate to all derived states and be hardened into an enforced verification gate so the same stale content cannot be re-exposed.
principleDraft.rationale: The root cause was the absence of a mandatory gate treating the source file's mtime+content as the fact source: a stale 08:12 session record was merged into CURRENT_FOCUS v48 without reading narration_lines_ep002.json, which the user had corrected at 08:24; three inspection rounds (16:46–18:46) claimed 'no change' from version/line metadata and memory alone; the stale theme was broadcast at 19:08 and the user had to correct it a second time at 19:19. Requiring actual source verification at every propagation path — merge, inspection, broadcast — and converting first corrections into enforced gates closes every route by which stale data survives. This operationalizes T-03 (observable evidence) and T-08 (corrections become improvements) for persistent-artifact synchronization rather than contradicting them.
applicability: Cross-session or cross-state merges and synchronizations against a persistent authoritative artifact (e.g., heartbeat merges into a focus/state file)
Periodic inspections and any 'no change' assertion about an authoritative source artifact
Pre-broadcast or pre-report consistency checks for content derived from a persistent artifact
Immediately after any human correction to an authoritative source: propagation to all derived states and hardening into enforced verification gates
antiPatterns: Merging prior session memory or historical records into current state without comparing the source artifact's actual mtime and content
Asserting 'no change' from version numbers, line counts, or session memory without reading the source artifact
Broadcasting content derived from state (e.g., a theme or topic) without a final consistency check against the current source
Recording a human correction only as a note (e.g., _meta.note) without enforcing it as a verification gate and propagating it to derived states
Treating derived or cached state as authoritative when it conflicts with the source artifact

parsed.thesis: Truth about a system's state lives in the authoritative source's current observable condition, not in memory, version counters, or historical records. Every cross-session merge, periodic inspection conclusion, or user-facing claim must be re-grounded in fresh direct observation of the source at the moment of decision; a record older than the source it describes must never silently overwrite newer truth, and explicit corrections must propagate as highest authority to all dependent state.

principleCandidate.title: Gate every state merge or no-change claim on direct comparison with the authoritative source's current state
principleCandidate.rationale: The root cause across all candidates was stale records being treated as authoritative: merges inherited old entries, inspections declared 'no changes' from memory and version counters, and a user correction was archived but not propagated. Forcing an mtime/content comparison against the source before any merge, inspection verdict, or broadcast makes stale-state overwrite structurally impossible rather than dependent on agent diligence, and elevates explicit corrections above all inferred or historical state.
principleCandidate.scope: Applies whenever cached, derived, or session-held state is merged across sessions, checked during periodic inspections, or used to produce user-facing claims about an authoritative source (files, databases, external systems). Especially relevant where user corrections may have altered the source after the cached state was formed.

risks: Partially overlaps with T-03 (use observable evidence before claiming results); this principle is a stricter operationalization specific to source-vs-cache authority and merge gating, but adoption should reference T-03 rather than replace it

Treating a single source file as sole authority can misfire when legitimate authority also lives elsewhere (e.g., user corrections recorded in metadata); an explicit authority hierarchy must be defined or corrections outside the file may be ignored

Mandating mtime+content-hash comparison on every heartbeat or merge adds latency and I/O cost; on high-frequency loops this may require sampling or change-notification mechanisms that reintroduce staleness windows

Rigid mechanical comparison (mtime/hash) verifies bytes, not semantics—a reformatted or timestamp-touched file with identical meaning could trigger unnecessary state resets, while meaning-level divergence in unmonitored fields could still pass the gate

principleDraft.title: Gate every state merge and no-change claim on fresh comparison with the authoritative source
principleDraft.statement: Before any cross-session state merge, periodic inspection verdict (e.g., a 'no changes' claim), or user-facing broadcast derived from cached state, the agent must freshly observe the authoritative source itself — at minimum comparing mtime and content against the cached record at the moment of decision — and treat that observation, not memory, version counters, or historical records, as the final authority. A record older than the source it describes must never silently overwrite the source's newer state, and an explicit user correction, once observed in the source, must propagate as the highest authority to all dependent state (focus files, inspection baselines, pending outputs).
principleDraft.rationale: The root cause was a missing validation gate, not insufficient diligence: the 12:00 heartbeat merged an 08:12 session record into CURRENT_FOCUS v48 without reading narration_lines_ep002.json, which the user had corrected at 08:24; the 16:46/17:46/18:46 inspections then declared 'no changes' from the v48/28-line counter and session memory alone, so the stale theme survived to the 19:08 broadcast and forced a second user correction at 19:19. Gating merges, inspection verdicts, and broadcasts on a fresh source comparison makes stale-record overwrite structurally impossible rather than dependent on agent recall, which had already failed twice in the same day.
applicability: Cross-session or cross-agent merges/syncs of cached or derived state into current state files (e.g., merging another agent's record into CURRENT_FOCUS)
Periodic heartbeat or inspection cycles that emit 'no change' / 'no update' verdicts about an authoritative source file, database, or external system
User-facing broadcasts or summaries whose content is derived from cached state about an authoritative source
Situations where a user correction may have modified the source after the cached state was formed (including corrections recorded in-file, e.g., _meta.note)
antiPatterns: Merging another session's or agent's historical record into current state without first comparing the authoritative source's current mtime/content
Declaring 'no changes' or 'no updates' from version counters, line counts, or session memory without reading the source
Broadcasting content derived from cached state that a user correction has since invalidated
Archiving a user correction (e.g., only in _meta.note) without propagating it to dependent state, inspection baselines, and pending outputs
Allowing a record older than the source it describes to silently overwrite the source's newer truth

intentContract.ownerIntent: The Owner wants the agent to never repeat an already-corrected fact: merges, inspection verdicts, and broadcasts must reflect the authoritative source's current content, so a correction given once (08:24) never has to be given again (19:19).
intentContract.targetBehavior: Before each cross-session merge, heartbeat inspection, or user-facing broadcast, the agent performs a fresh direct read of the authoritative source (mtime/content compared against cached state), updates dependent state to match the source on mismatch, and treats any explicit user correction found in the source as top authority for all dependent records.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Concluding 'no changes', merging, or broadcasting based on memory, version counters, line counts, or historical records without directly comparing the authoritative source's current content — the failure family that let a stale episode theme survive a user correction and be re-broadcast the same day.

intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should accept a rule only if it requires an observable source read (mtime/content) before any merge, before any 'no-change' verdict, and before any broadcast; forbids memory/counter-based conclusions; and requires propagation of explicit corrections to dependent state. A rule that lets a stale record survive the comparison, or lets a correction remain archived-only, fails this intent.

risks: Overlaps with T-03 (and partially T-02/T-05); this principle is a stricter operationalization for source-vs-cache authority and merge gating — downstream rules should reference those axioms rather than replace them

Byte-level gating (mtime/content hash) verifies bytes, not semantics: reformatting or timestamp touches with identical meaning can trigger unnecessary state resets, while semantic drift in unmonitored fields can pass the gate
Mandatory mtime+content comparison on every heartbeat adds I/O and latency; high-frequency loops may adopt sampling or change notifications that reopen staleness windows

The correction-propagation mandate can conflict with T-06 (change no more state than necessary) if applied as blanket rewrites; propagation should stay scoped to state that depends on the corrected fact

Inherited records, session memory, and version/line-count heuristics are merely caches: without re-verification against the source's actual content, corrected errors are silently re-imported and propagate, and user corrections are lost unless they are persisted and converted into mandatory pre-action checks.

principleDraft.title: Re-verify the authoritative source before merging or claiming state is unchanged
principleDraft.statement: Before performing any cross-session or cross-component state merge, sync, inspection, or report—and specifically before outputting any 'no new changes' conclusion or inheriting a prior record—the agent must observe the authoritative source object directly (mtime plus actual content) within the same action. Inherited records, session memory, and version/line-count heuristics are caches, not evidence: on any discrepancy the source's observed content prevails, the difference is recorded, and user corrections are persisted as explicit baselines so they cannot be silently overwritten or re-corrected.
principleDraft.rationale: The root failure was a synchronization flow with no mandatory source-first verification gate: the 12:00 heartbeat merged the stale 08:12 main-agent record (episode 2 = trust version, 30 clips) into CURRENT_FOCUS v48 without reading narration_lines_ep002.json, which the user had already corrected at 08:24 (10-principles overview, 15 clips, recorded in _meta.note). Three subsequent inspections (16:46, 17:46, 18:46) then claimed 'no new changes' based only on session memory and the v48/28-line heuristic, letting the stale theme propagate into the 19:08 broadcast and forcing a second user correction at 19:19. Requiring a fresh read of the source at the moment of action breaks this propagation path: stale records cannot be silently re-imported, no-change claims become evidence-based, and persisted correction baselines make repeated user corrections unnecessary.
applicability: Cross-session or cross-component state merges and syncs (e.g., a heartbeat merging an earlier main-agent record into a CURRENT_FOCUS state file)
Periodic heartbeat inspections that compare current state against a previous observation and may conclude 'no new changes'
Broadcast, summary, or report generation whose content derives from an authoritative source file (e.g., narration_lines_ep002.json driving a scheduled broadcast)
Any action about to inherit a prior record, historical state file, or version/line-count heuristic as authoritative without having observed the source in the current action
antiPatterns: Merging a stale or cross-session record into current state without reading the source object's actual content in the same action, silently re-importing corrected errors
Declaring 'no new changes' from session memory, version numbers, or line counts (e.g., 'CURRENT_FOCUS still v48/28 lines') instead of comparing the source's mtime and content
Treating an inherited record or cached state as authoritative when it conflicts with the source's observed content
Leaving a user correction unpersisted so the same error recurs and the user must correct it again (the 08:24 and 19:19 double correction of the episode-2 theme)

intentContract.ownerIntent: The Owner wants the actual content of the authoritative source file to be the final authority during state sync, so stale records are never merged or broadcast and the Owner never has to make the same correction twice.
intentContract.targetBehavior: In any merge, sync, inspection, or report action, the agent's tool trajectory shows a fresh read of the authoritative source (mtime and content) performed within that same action before state is merged or a 'no new changes' claim is output, with discrepancies resolved in favor of the source and user corrections persisted as explicit baselines.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Asserting that state is unchanged, or merging inherited records into current state, based solely on session memory, version numbers, or line counts without observing the authoritative source's current content in the action being performed.
intentContract.evidenceSource: Diagnosis diagnosis_manual_1788609453041_dtmlftov: the 12:00 heartbeat merged the stale 08:12 record (episode 2 = trust version, 30 clips) into CURRENT_FOCUS v48 without checking narration_lines_ep002.json, which the user had corrected at 08:24 (10-principles overview, 15 clips, noted in _meta.note); the 16:46/17:46/18:46 inspections then claimed 'no new changes' on memory and the v48/28-line heuristic, propagating the stale theme into the 19:08 broadcast and forcing a second user correction at 19:19.
intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should accept only rules that require an observable source read (mtime and content) within the same action as any merge or no-change claim, that make the source prevail on conflict, and that persist corrections as explicit baselines; any rule that permits memory-based or version-heuristic 'no change' claims contradicts this intent and must be flagged rather than merged.

risks: Partially overlaps core axiom T-03 (use observable evidence before claiming results) and touches T-08/T-10; this is a specialization for cross-session state synchronization, so downstream rule generation must scope rules to sync/merge/no-change-claim contexts to avoid duplicating existing axioms.

Mandatory fresh reads (mtime plus content hash) on every heartbeat or merge add I/O and latency; applied indiscriminately to many or large sources it becomes wasteful, so freshness checks may need sensible intervals or change-notification support without removing the gate.

Treating the source as absolute authority can lose legitimate corrections still held in memory or queues and not yet written to the source, causing oscillation; correction write-through must be atomic with the source update.
A hard pre-action gate can stall workflows when the source is temporarily unreadable; the fail-safe path must be block-and-alert, never proceed on assumption.
Over-rigid content comparison may flag benign structural changes (e.g., reformatting) as conflicts, generating false alarms and eroding trust in the guardrail.
